text: With credentials configured, every AWS CLI command follows the same shape: aws, a service name, a command, and any parameters. Recognize that pattern and most AWS CLI calls become readable on sight, even ones you've never typed before.

aws ec2 describe-instances lists EC2 instances. aws s3 ls lists your buckets, or the objects inside one if you give it a bucket URI. aws s3 cp uploads a local file straight to S3. aws iam list-users lists IAM users. The service name tells you which API you're calling, the command tells you the action, and once you know a handful of each, you can often guess the command you need for something new — the same discoverability idea as the Azure CLI's az pattern from the prerequisite course.

Every aws command returns JSON by default. --output reformats that for how you're working: table gives human-readable columns while you're reading results at a terminal, text strips the formatting down to plain tab-separated lines a shell script can loop over, and json stays the default because it's what the CLI itself operates on before --output ever touches it.

An account with forty running instances returns forty objects' worth of detail you probably don't need all of. --query applies a JMESPath expression to that raw JSON before --output formats it. But the query has to match how AWS actually nests the data: describe-instances doesn't return a flat list of instances, it returns a list of Reservations, and each reservation holds a nested list of Instances. Reservations[].Instances[] flattens both levels, and the {ID:InstanceId, Type:InstanceType, State:State.Name} part picks out just three fields per instance, including the nested State.Name, out of the dozens each one actually has.

Local AWS CLI commands work anywhere you've installed and configured the tool. Lesson 19 introduces AWS CloudShell, a browser-based shell that's already authenticated and already has the CLI installed, plus a first real script that loops over your own resources.
